Raw Accelerometry Tutorial

Published

September 5, 2025

This tutorial will focus on generating minute-level Activity Counts1 and steps from an ActiGraph GT3X file. While this pipeline is not comprehensive, it includes the basic steps that are necessary to process raw accelerometry data into minute-level summaries.

Note

The .gt3x file format is used by ActiGraph accelerometers and contains raw accelerometer data along with metadata including timestamps and device information. Accelerometry data may be provided in other formats, such as .csv, but will typically include timestamps, values for acceleration in the X, Y, and Z dimensions, and metadata like participant ID.

First, we download a GT3X file from the ActiGraph website. The file contains approximately one day of data.

Download file

gt3x_file_raw = here::here("data", "accel_data_raw", "GT3X+ (01 day).gt3x")
gt3x_file = here::here("data", "accel_data_raw", "sample_data.gt3x")

if(!file.exists(gt3x_file)){
  url = "http://dl.theactigraph.com/demo/files/GT3XPlus-RawData(1-20).zip"

  out_file = here::here("data", "accel_data_raw.zip")
  if(!file.exists(out_file)){
    curl::curl_download(url, out_file, mode = "wb")
  }
  
  zip_file = here::here("data", "accel_data_raw.zip")
  out_dir  = here::here("data", "accel_data_raw")
  
  if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) {
    dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)
  }
  
  zip_list = unzip(zip_file, list = TRUE)
  
  unzip(zip_file, files = zip_list[1]$Name, exdir = out_dir)
  file.rename(gt3x_file_raw, gt3x_file)
}

Read in the data

We read in the data using the read.gt3x package. We read in as a dataframe instead of matrix (asDataFrame = TRUE) and impute any missing values with zeroes (imputeZeroes = TRUE). The read.gt3x::read.gt3x function will read in the data and return a data.frame with columns for time, X, Y, Z, and other metadata. The time column is in POSIXct format.

df = read.gt3x::read.gt3x(path = gt3x_file,
                          asDataFrame = TRUE,
                          imputeZeroes = TRUE)

Get to know the data

The columns in the data are time, X, Y, and Z. Regardless of whether the data came from a GT3X file or other format, the next steps assume the data is in a data.frame format with columns for timestamp and the three acceleration axes.

head(df)
Sampling Rate: 30Hz
Firmware Version: 2.5.0
Serial Number Prefix: NEO
                 time X Y Z
1 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0
2 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0
3 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0
4 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0
5 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0
6 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0

The data frame also has attributes that provide additional information about the data. The most important attributes are sample_rate and acceleration_min/acceleration_max. Many functions for processing the raw data require the sample_rate; alternatively, the sample rate can be estimated from the timestamps if they are uniform. The acceleration_min and acceleration_max attributes provide the minimum and maximum acceleration values that the device can measure, which is important for calculating minute-level metrics like Activity Counts or Monitor Independent Movement Summary (MIMS).

attributes(df) %>% names
 [1] "names"            "row.names"        "class"            "subject_name"    
 [5] "light_data"       "old_version"      "firmware"         "last_sample_time"
 [9] "serial_prefix"    "sample_rate"      "acceleration_min" "acceleration_max"
[13] "header"           "start_time"       "stop_time"        "bad_samples"     
attr(df, "sample_rate")
[1] 30
Tip

When working with sub-second level data, make sure to set option digits.secs = 3. This allows us to make sure that milliseconds haven’t been truncated. Truncation can occur during conversion from timestamp types or when writing and then reading from other data formats (e.g. CSV). Failure to account for milliseconds properly can cause problems when joining/merging based on timestamps.

options(digits.secs = 3)
head(df$time)
[1] "2012-06-27 10:54:00.000 GMT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00.033 GMT"
[3] "2012-06-27 10:54:00.066 GMT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00.099 GMT"
[5] "2012-06-27 10:54:00.133 GMT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00.166 GMT"

A note on time zones

When using the read.gt3x package, the time zone of the output data is always GMT. Which time zone the data were collected may be contained in the header; in this case however, it is not.

attr_list = attributes(df)
attr_list$header$TimeZone
NULL
Important

All timestamps are in local time (of the device) even though they are represented as POSIXct with GMT timezone [in the data]; see documentation here. Let’s go through an explicit example.

  • A user starts recording data with a GT3X device at 8AM in New York City in June (Eastern Daylight Time Zone, UTC-6).
  • In the data, the timestamp will be recorded as 08:00 GMT

You can set the data to the correct timezone with lubridate::tz. The with_tz and force_tz functions can change the timestamp the data in different ways (changing attribute vs. changing data).

Here we illustrate the difference between changing the attribute and changing the data. Let’s take a subset of the times and show the time zone (GMT).

times = head(df$time)
times
[1] "2012-06-27 10:54:00.000 GMT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00.033 GMT"
[3] "2012-06-27 10:54:00.066 GMT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00.099 GMT"
[5] "2012-06-27 10:54:00.133 GMT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00.166 GMT"
tz(times)
[1] "GMT"

The force_tz, and tz(x) <- functions assign a specified timezone to the object.

times_edt = times # make a copy of the times 
tz(times_edt) <- "America/New_York"; times_edt
[1] "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT"
[3] "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT"
[5] "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT"
force_tz(times, "America/New_York")
[1] "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT"
[3] "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT"
[5] "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT" "2012-06-27 10:54:00 EDT"

We see that the result is the time itself hasn’t changed but the time zone attachd is EDT instead of GMT. Tge data still indicates hour minute 10:54, but in a different timezone.

The with_tz function projects the data into a timezone, but the actual moment of time does not change:

with_tz(times, "America/New_York")
[1] "2012-06-27 06:54:00 EDT" "2012-06-27 06:54:00 EDT"
[3] "2012-06-27 06:54:00 EDT" "2012-06-27 06:54:00 EDT"
[5] "2012-06-27 06:54:00 EDT" "2012-06-27 06:54:00 EDT"

Now the data displays hour 06:54 as this shifts the data from GMT. We can see that force_tz doesn’t change the way the data is stored, just the way it is displayed, but with_tz changes the way the data is both stored and displayed.

as.numeric(times_edt)
[1] 1340808840 1340808840 1340808840 1340808840 1340808840 1340808840
as.numeric(force_tz(times, "America/New_York"))
[1] 1340808840 1340808840 1340808840 1340808840 1340808840 1340808840
as.numeric(with_tz(times, "America/New_York"))
[1] 1340794440 1340794440 1340794440 1340794440 1340794440 1340794440
Warning

Takehome message: Use caution with time zones, especially in the presence of data from different devices and when merging data with timestamps, such as merging with GPS or heart rate data. Shifting time may project some data into a different day/date, which is highly relevant since many summary measures are done at a day/date level. Non-GT3X files and packages other than read.gt3x may handle time zones differently, so be sure to check the documentation.

Plotting the data

Before we do anything else, let’s plot the data. We have 2699958 observations, so we’ll want to start with plotting a subset only. We pivot the data longer for easier plotting and plot the first five minutes of observations.

long = df %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = X:Z, names_to = "axis", values_to = "accel")

long %>% 
  filter(between(time, floor_date(time[1]), #keep only first 5 minutes
                   floor_date(time[1]) + as.period(5, "minutes"))) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = accel, colour = axis)) + 
    geom_line() + # add acceleration, can also do `geom_step`
    theme(legend.position = "inside", 
          legend.position.inside = c(0.6, 0.78),
          panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  paletteer::scale_color_paletteer_d("ggthemr::flat", name = "Axis") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "1 min")+
  labs(y = "Acceleration (g)", x = "Time")

We see that at the beginning of the data, all acceleration values are zero. We’ll discuss this in the context of idle sleep mode.

Handling idle sleep mode

Idle sleep mode is an option for ActiGraph devices set when recording. When a device hasn’t moved for a period of time, it does not record any measurements until the device moves again. This is done to preserve battery life.

ActiGraph documentation explains idle sleep mode as follows:

For example, a device set to sample at 30Hz would store the last known accelerometer reading 30 times every second; the device would then wake up and check for movement. If no movement were detected, this pattern would continue. Otherwise the unit would exit sleep mode (i.e., “wake up”) and continue sampling in normal fashion.

Thus, if idle sleep mode activates on a device, there will be a gap in time in the measurements. While this is an accurate representation of the data, it causes issues for methods that rely on continuous measurements. The imputeZeroes argument in read.gt3x fills in missing measurements with 0 for all axes. This zeroes are not always from idle sleep mode: for example, they could also be from charging events. The flag_idle_sleep (default FALSE) argument in read.gt3x outputs an indicator column of idle or not and is useful for identifying segments of data that are in idle sleep mode. We see that the first few seconds of our data are in idle sleep mode:

df_flagged = read.gt3x::read.gt3x(path = gt3x_file, 
                                  asDataFrame = TRUE, 
                                  imputeZeroes = TRUE,
                                  flag_idle_sleep = TRUE)
head(df_flagged)
Sampling Rate: 30Hz
Firmware Version: 2.5.0
Serial Number Prefix: NEO
                 time X Y Z idle
1 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0 TRUE
2 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0 TRUE
3 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0 TRUE
4 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0 TRUE
5 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0 TRUE
6 2012-06-27 10:54:00 0 0 0 TRUE
long_flag = df_flagged %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = X:Z, names_to = "axis", values_to = "accel")

idle_df = df_flagged %>% 
  filter(between(time, floor_date(time[1]), #keep only first 5 minutes
                   floor_date(time[1]) + as.period(5, "minutes"))) %>% 
  filter(idle == TRUE) 

long_flag %>% 
  filter(between(time, floor_date(time[1]), #keep only first 5 minutes
                   floor_date(time[1]) + as.period(5, "minutes"))) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = accel, colour = axis)) + 
    geom_line() + # add acceleration, can also do `geom_step`
    annotate(geom = "rect",
             xmin = min(idle_df$time),
             xmax = max(idle_df$time),
             ymin = -3,
             ymax = 3,
             fill = "pink", 
             alpha = .8) +
    theme(legend.position = "inside", 
          legend.position.inside = c(0.6, 0.78),
          panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  paletteer::scale_color_paletteer_d("ggthemr::flat", name = "Axis") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "1 min")+
  labs(y = "Acceleration (g)", x = "Time")

There’s also at least one more instance of idle sleep mode:

idle_df_notstart = df_flagged %>% 
  filter(!between(time, floor_date(time[1]), #keep only first 5 minutes
                   floor_date(time[1]) + as.period(5, "minutes"))) %>% 
  filter(idle == TRUE) 

segments_idle = 
  idle_df_notstart %>% 
  mutate(lag = as.numeric(difftime(time, lag(time), units = "secs")),
         lag = lag < .05,
         group = data.table::rleid(lag))


##11:20 to 11:50
long %>% 
  filter(between(time, as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 11:20:00", tz = "GMT"),
                 as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 11:50:00", tz = "GMT"))) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = accel, colour = axis)) + 
    geom_line() + # add acceleration, can also do `geom_step`
    annotate(geom = "rect",
             xmin = min(segments_idle$time[segments_idle$group == 2]),
             xmax = max(segments_idle$time[segments_idle$group == 2]),
             ymin = -3,
             ymax = 3,
             fill = "pink", 
             alpha = .7) +
    theme(legend.position = "inside", 
          legend.position.inside = c(0.6, 0.9),
          panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  paletteer::scale_color_paletteer_d("ggthemr::flat", name = "Axis") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "5 min")+
  labs(y = "Acceleration (g)", x = "Time")

There are a few options for handling data in idle sleep mode:

  • Leave gaps in the data
  • Fill in NA values for these segments
  • Fill in 0 values for these segments,
  • Last observation carried forward (LOCF)
Method Issues
Leave gaps in data Most software assumes continuous time, missing time may cause errors
Fill in NA values Some software assumes no missing data
Fill in 0 values Not accurate because gravity is being exerted on the device, can cause sharp changes in the signal which can induce higher variance than is correct (going from value to 0)
Last observation carried forward (LOCF) Not “real” values, harder to identify non-wear after the fact if not flagged appropriately
Note

The LOCF approach is such that if the last measurement before non-measurement on an axis was 0.952 for example, the value of 0.952 will be repeated for each sample until the device moves. Each axis is handled separately (no information for X is used for Y). This procedure is done for all axes.

Our recommendation is to use the LOCF approach. It is consistent with the ActiGraph documentation, induces a variance of 0 during the idle sleep interval, has no jump discontinuity from previous measurements, provides continuous signal, and can be flagged. Summary measures of activity (e.g. Activity Counts, Activity Index) should provide an appropriate summary value of \(0\) to this zero variance data.

There are packages that implement LOCF on this type of data, but we can also do it using some straightforward tidyverse functions. We find records where all axes have an acceleration of \(0\), replace those acceleration values for those records with NA and fill in the data (using LOCF) using tidyr::fill.

sample_rate = attr(df, "sample_rate")
acceleration_max = as.numeric(attr(df, "acceleration_max"))
df = dplyr::as_tibble(df)
df = df %>% 
  mutate(all_zero = X == 0 & Y == 0 & Z == 0) %>%  # flag where all zeroes
  mutate( # replace all 0 with NA so it can be filled  
    X = ifelse(all_zero, NA_real_, X),
    Y = ifelse(all_zero, NA_real_, Y),
    Z = ifelse(all_zero, NA_real_, Z)
  )
any(df$all_zero)
[1] TRUE
df = df %>% 
  select(-all_zero) %>% # remove this column
  tidyr::fill(X, Y, Z, .direction = "down") # fill down using LOCF (time sorted)
head(df)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  time                        X     Y     Z
  <dttm>                  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 2012-06-27 10:54:00.000    NA    NA    NA
2 2012-06-27 10:54:00.033    NA    NA    NA
3 2012-06-27 10:54:00.066    NA    NA    NA
4 2012-06-27 10:54:00.099    NA    NA    NA
5 2012-06-27 10:54:00.133    NA    NA    NA
6 2012-06-27 10:54:00.166    NA    NA    NA

If the first records are in idle sleep mode, they will have no “before value” to fill in and will continue to be NA given this code. To handle this last case we can replace these values using tidyr::fill with the direction of “up” to make a flat starting signal or with \(0\) for simplicity (done here):

df = df %>% tidyr::replace_na(list(X = 0, Y = 0, Z = 0))

This ensures that every record has a numeric value. Users can also drop those first records.

Now we can see that the signal has been filled in for those segments that were previously all \(0\).

long = df %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = X:Z, names_to = "axis", values_to = "accel")

long %>% 
  filter(between(time, as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 11:20:00", tz = "GMT"),
                 as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 11:50:00", tz = "GMT"))) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = accel, colour = axis)) + 
    geom_line() + # add acceleration, can also do `geom_step`
    annotate(geom = "rect",
             xmin = min(segments_idle$time[segments_idle$group == 2]),
             xmax = max(segments_idle$time[segments_idle$group == 2]),
             ymin = -3,
             ymax = 3,
             fill = "pink", 
             alpha = .7) +
    theme(legend.position = "inside", 
          legend.position.inside = c(0.6, 0.9),
          panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  paletteer::scale_color_paletteer_d("ggthemr::flat", name = "Axis") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "5 min")+
  labs(y = "Acceleration (g)", x = "Time")

Gravity Calibration

Gravity correction/calibration corrects issues in the data that may arise from miscalibration of a device. Accelerometry is measured in \(g\), and we assume that gravity values for each person are the same if another device was used or the same device was used at a different location. Thus gravity correction can help harmonize data that is different due to non-biological or systemic effects.

The most common gravity correction method estimates shift and scale parameters to transform the data and will therefore only affect downstream metrics that are not invariant to scaling and shifting. The correction should be small compared to the magnitude of the signal.

Note

Not all pipelines employ gravity correction, including many pipelines for ActiGraph data.

We will use the method employed in GGIR2.

More about gravity calibration

The calibration is done by estimating how much of the data is projected onto the unit sphere (radius of length 1 for all 3 axes).

The procedure below looks for when the standard deviation of the signal was <13 m\(g\) (milli-\(g\)) in all three axes within a time window. The 13 m\(g\) cutoff was selected to be just above the empirically derived baseline (noise) standard deviation of 10 m\(g\) to retain only non-movement periods. A window of length 10 seconds is used.

The GGIR::g.calibrate function takes in a data filename and calculates the calibration parameters. We recommend to input the output of g.inspectfile that provides metadata and a specification of the file being calibrated. Since we have an older GT3X file that can’t be directly read in by GGIR, we first use the SummarizedActigraphy package to write to csv, then use GGIR for calibration. We use imputeZeroes=FALSE because we don’t want the calibration to use any data from idle sleep mode.

We can download the SummarizedActigraphy package from Github first:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("muschellij2/SummarizedActigraphy")

Then apply calibration:

library(GGIR)
df_nozero = read.gt3x::read.gt3x(path = gt3x_file, 
                      asDataFrame = TRUE,
                      imputeZeroes = FALSE)

outfile = SummarizedActigraphy::write_acc_csv(df_nozero, 
                                              tempfile(fileext = ".csv"))
info = GGIR::g.inspectfile(outfile)
csv_calibration_params = GGIR::g.calibrate(
  datafile = outfile,
  inspectfileobject = info)

Loading chunk: 1 2 3

The parameters denotes how many hours of data was used:

csv_calibration_params$nhoursused
[1] 23.00556

What the estimated calibration error was for all non-movement windows before and after calibration to the unit sphere:

csv_calibration_params$cal.error.start
[1] 0.01387
csv_calibration_params$cal.error.end
NULL

In this case, we see that:

csv_calibration_params$QCmessage
[1] "recalibration not done because not enough points on all sides of the sphere"

Therefore the scale and shift parameters are \(1\) and \(0\) in all three dimensions:

csv_calibration_params[c("scale", "offset")]
$scale
[1] 1 1 1

$offset
[1] 0 0 0

We’ll still illustrate how to calibrate the data by using the scale function and performing the subtraction/division:

df_calibrated = df
df_calibrated[, c("X", "Y", "Z")] = scale(
  df[, c("X", "Y", "Z")], 
  center = -csv_calibration_params$offset, 
  scale = 1/csv_calibration_params$scale)

Calculating Activity Counts

Activity Counts (AC) are a measure of physical activity. Previously they were a proprietary output of the ActiLife software, but the ActiGraph team published a paper in 2022 that describes how they are calculated and released the agcounts Python module to calculate them3. The agcounts, actilifecounts, and agcounter packages have functions that can convert the raw data into minute-level counts. The actilifecounts implements the method in native R code, agcounts/agcounter wraps the Python code into an R interface.

Calculating AC from these packages gives a per-axis AC measure. Axis-level AC can be aggregated from higher resolutions to lower: if you calculate AC at 15 second intervals, then the 60 second/minute level AC is the sum of the 4 values measured at 15 seconds. Once AC is aggregated at the desired epoch, the AC units from the axes are combined into a vector magnitude for a single summary:

\[ AC = \sqrt{(AC_{x}^2 + AC_{y}^2 + AC_{z}^2)} \]

Typically, we calculate counts for 60-second (1 minute) epochs. We can pass in the timezone of the data to ensure the desired time stamps. We use the calibrated data and have to first convert to data frame, then rename columns for consistency.

df_calibrated = df_calibrated %>% 
  as.data.frame()
ac60 = df_calibrated %>% 
  agcounts::calculate_counts(epoch = 60L, tz = lubridate::tz(df_calibrated$time))
head(ac60)
                 time Axis1 Axis2 Axis3 Vector.Magnitude
1 2012-06-27 10:54:00   207   218   270              404
2 2012-06-27 10:55:00   169   257   270              409
3 2012-06-27 10:56:00     0     0     0                0
4 2012-06-27 10:57:00   157   174   248              341
5 2012-06-27 10:58:00    23    23   279              281
6 2012-06-27 10:59:00     0     0     0                0
ac60 = 
  ac60 %>% 
  select(time, AC = Vector.Magnitude, everything())

# save for later analysis 
out_dir = here::here("data", "accel_outputs")
if(!dir.exists(out_dir)) dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)

out_file = here::here(out_dir, "minute_level_ac.rds")
if(!file.exists(out_file)) {
  readr::write_rds(ac60,
                   out_file,
                   compress = "xz")
}
Note

The AC algorithm resamples the data to 30Hz. The original algorithm provided in the agcounts Python module only correctly handled sample rates that were measured at round intervals (e.g. 30, 40, …, 90, 100).

Let’s plot the AC with some thresholds for physical activity levels. While many different thresholds can be used, the Montoye4 thresholds are a common choice.

More about thresholds

The Montoye thresholds were developed by observing \(n=47\) participants in both laboratory and free-living settings. Activity intensity was determined through direct observation and then mapped to the AC measured by wrist-worn accelerometers to develop cut points for each activity intensity. The cut points had an accuracy of \(70\)% in free-living. The Montoye thresholds are specific to Activity Counts, but another paper has mapped the AC thresholds to other activity summaries, including Monitor Independent Movement Summaries (MIMS; see below) and Euclidian Norm Minus One (ENMO)5.

ac60 %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = AC)) + 
  geom_line() +
  annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 0,
           ymax = 2860,
           fill = "#3498DBFF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
  annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 2861,
           ymax = 3940,
           fill = "#F39C12FF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
   annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 3941,
           ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#E74C3CFF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "Activity Counts (AC)", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 1430,
           label = "Sedentary") + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 3300,
           label = "Light") + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 7000,
           label = "Moderate-vigorous")

Calculating other outputs

MIMS

Monitor Independent Movement Summary (MIMS)6 are an open-source summary of physical activity. They were used in the NHANES accelerometry study from 2011-20147. We can calculate MIMS using the MIMSunit package; this requires acceleration_max variables from the header.

dynamic_range = c(-acceleration_max, acceleration_max)
df_mims = df_calibrated %>% 
  rename(HEADER_TIME_STAMP = time) %>% 
  MIMSunit::mims_unit(dynamic_range = dynamic_range, epoch = "1 min")
================================================
================================
## save for later analysis 
out_file = here::here(out_dir, "minute_level_mims.rds")
if(!file.exists(out_file)) {
  readr::write_rds(df_mims %>% rename(time = HEADER_TIME_STAMP, mims = MIMS_UNIT),
                   out_file,
                   compress = "xz")
}

Note, as this resamples data to 100Hz, this may have a significantly larger memory footprint for processing than the raw data. We can see the output from the MIMS processing:

head(df_mims)
    HEADER_TIME_STAMP MIMS_UNIT
1 2012-06-27 10:54:00 17.026593
2 2012-06-27 10:55:00  2.936831
3 2012-06-27 10:56:00  3.159907
4 2012-06-27 10:57:00  0.000000
5 2012-06-27 10:58:00  3.299991
6 2012-06-27 10:59:00  1.169498

We can plot the MIMS, using thresholds mapped from the AC thresholds8.

df_mims %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = HEADER_TIME_STAMP, y = MIMS_UNIT)) + 
  geom_line() +
  annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 0,
           ymax = 15.047,
           fill = "#3498DBFF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
  annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 15.048,
           ymax = 19.614,
           fill = "#F39C12FF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
   annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 19.615,
           ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#E74C3CFF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
  labs(y = "MIMS", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 8,
           label = "Sedentary") + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 17,
           label = "Light") + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 23,
           label = "Moderate-vigorous") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "MIMS", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

Steps

Steps can be estimated from raw accelerometry data using several different open source algorithms. Here we’ll focus on two algorithms: the machine learning based stepcount algorithm, which is implemented in Python. The Python module provides two machine learning algorithms (self-supervised learner [SSL] and random forest [RF]) that estimate steps from raw accelerometry.

The stepcount R package wraps this Python code. The package also has functions for creating a Conda environment for these functions, as many different Python modules have different requirements - the walking package has similar functionality.

You need to first create the conda environment:

library(stepcount)
envname = "stepcount"
reticulate::conda_create(envname = envname, packages = c("python=3.9", "openjdk", "pip"))
Sys.unsetenv("RETICULATE_PYTHON")
reticulate::use_condaenv(envname)
reticulate::py_install("stepcount", envname = envname, method = "conda", pip = TRUE)

Then we can check we have everything in order:

stepcount::unset_reticulate_python()
stepcount::use_stepcount_condaenv()
library(reticulate)
stepcount::stepcount_check() 
[1] TRUE

Then we can run the model, using the SSL model type. We have to include the sample rate as well. Since the method does it’s own gravity calibration, we use the uncalibrated dataset. To make knitting faster, we save the output.

out = here::here("tutorials", "data", "sc_out.rds")
if(!dir.exists(dirname(out))) dir.create(dirname(out))

if(!file.exists(out)){
  ssl = stepcount::stepcount(df, sample_rate = sample_rate, model_type = "ssl")
  readr::write_rds(ssl, out)
}
ssl = readr::read_rds(out)

The output of stepcount is a list of different pieces of information, including information about the device:

names(ssl)
[1] "steps"      "walking"    "step_times" "info"

We are most interested in the data.frame of estimated steps with associated timestamps:

head(ssl$steps)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  time                    steps
  <dttm>                  <dbl>
1 2012-06-27 10:54:00.000     0
2 2012-06-27 10:54:10.000     0
3 2012-06-27 10:54:20.000     0
4 2012-06-27 10:54:30.000     0
5 2012-06-27 10:54:40.000     0
6 2012-06-27 10:54:50.000     0

and similarly a data.frame of flagged time for walking:

head(ssl$walking)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  time                    walking
  <dttm>                    <dbl>
1 2012-06-27 10:54:00.000       0
2 2012-06-27 10:54:10.000       0
3 2012-06-27 10:54:20.000       0
4 2012-06-27 10:54:30.000       0
5 2012-06-27 10:54:40.000       0
6 2012-06-27 10:54:50.000       0

The stepcount method estimates steps in 10-second windows, which we can aggregate into minutes:

ssl_60 = ssl$steps %>% 
  mutate(time = floor_date(time, "1 minute")) %>% 
  group_by(time) %>% 
  summarise(ssl_steps = sum(steps), .groups = "drop")
head(ssl_60)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  time                    ssl_steps
  <dttm>                      <dbl>
1 2012-06-27 10:54:00.000         0
2 2012-06-27 10:55:00.000         0
3 2012-06-27 10:56:00.000         0
4 2012-06-27 10:57:00.000         0
5 2012-06-27 10:58:00.000         0
6 2012-06-27 10:59:00.000         0

We can fit the random forest too:

out = here::here("tutorials", "data", "rf_out.rds")

if(!file.exists(out)){
  rf = stepcount::stepcount(df, sample_rate = sample_rate, model_type = "rf")
  readr::write_rds(rf, out)
}
rf = readr::read_rds(out)

rf_60 = 
  rf$steps %>% 
  mutate(time = floor_date(time, "1 minute")) %>% 
  group_by(time) %>% 
  summarise(rf_steps = sum(steps), .groups = "drop")

We can plot the results; we see a large difference between number steps identified by each method!

steps_joined = 
  rf_60 %>% 
  full_join(ssl_60, by = "time")

steps_joined %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = contains("steps"),
               names_to = "method", 
               values_to = "steps") %>% 
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = c("ssl_steps", "rf_steps"), labels = c("SSL", "RF"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = steps, color = method)) + 
  geom_step() +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "Steps per Minute", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#9B59B6FF", "#D35400FF"),
                     labels = c("SSL", "RF"),
                     name = "Method") + 
  facet_grid(method~.)

Finally, we can zoom in on a walking period:

joined_seconds =
  ssl$steps %>% rename(ssl_steps = steps) %>% 
  full_join(rf$steps %>% rename(rf_steps = steps), by = "time") %>% 
  filter(rf_steps > 0 & ssl_steps > 0)


xdf = 
  joined_seconds %>% 
  mutate(end = time + as.period(10, "seconds")) %>% 
  filter(time >= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:53:40", tz = "GMT") & 
         end <= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:54:40", tz = "GMT"))

p1 = df %>% 
  mutate(vm = sqrt(X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2)) %>% 
  filter(time >= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:53:50", tz = "GMT") & 
         time <= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:54:40", tz = "GMT")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = vm)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "5 secs", date_labels = "%H:%M:%S") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Time of day", y = "Acceleration (g)", title = "RF Steps") +
  geom_rect(data = xdf, 
            aes(xmin = time, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = rf_steps), 
             alpha = 0.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis(limits = c(9, 20), name = "Steps per 10 second window",
                              breaks = seq(10, 20, 2))

p2 = df %>% 
  mutate(vm = sqrt(X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2)) %>% 
  filter(time >= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:53:50", tz = "GMT") & 
         time <= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:54:40", tz = "GMT")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = vm)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "5 secs", date_labels = "%H:%M:%S") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Time of day", y = "Acceleration (g)", title = "SSL Steps") +
  geom_rect(data = xdf, 
            aes(xmin = time, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = ssl_steps), 
             alpha = 0.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis(limits = c(9, 20), name = "Steps per 10 second window",
                              breaks = seq(10, 20, 2))


p1 / p2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect", axes = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")

## save results for downstream analysis
out_file = here::here(out_dir, "minute_level_steps.rds")
if(!file.exists(out_file)) {
  readr::write_rds(steps_joined,
                   out_file,
                   compress = "xz")
}

Nonwear and Sleep

The actigraph.sleepr package implements three sleep scoring/detection algorithms: Sadeh9, Cole-Kripke10 and Tudor-Locke11 as well as two non-wear detection algorithms: Troiano12 and Choi13.

We can download the package from Github:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("dipetkov/actigraph.sleepr")

Nonwear

We will demonstrate using the Choi algorithm to find nonwear. We will run this on the minute-level AC data, not the raw accelerometry data.

We need to rename the time column to timestamp and make all column names lowercase.

data = ac60 %>%
  rename(timestamp = time) %>% 
  janitor::clean_names()
choi_nonwear = actigraph.sleepr::apply_choi(data, use_magnitude = TRUE)
head(choi_nonwear)
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  period_start        period_end          length
  <dttm>              <dttm>               <int>
1 2012-06-28 00:00:00 2012-06-28 02:36:00    156

The default for use_magnitude is FALSE, which means that only the axis1 is used to measure activity. We set use_magnitude = TRUE so that the magnitude of the vector (axis1, axis2, axis3) is used instead.

The output is a data.frame with the start and stop times of non-wear, along with the length of the nonwear interval.

We see that the output is a data.frame of start and stop times of non-wear. We can expand this to a sequence of times and merge with the minute level counts, creating a column with an indicator for wear.

if (nrow(choi_nonwear) == 0) {
  data$choi_wear = TRUE
} else {
  choi_df = purrr::map2_df(
    choi_nonwear$period_start, choi_nonwear$period_end,
    function(from, to) {
      data.frame(timestamp = seq(from, to, by = 60L), # need this name to align
                 choi_wear = FALSE)
    })
  data = left_join(data, choi_df) %>%
    tidyr::replace_na(list(choi_wear = TRUE)) # default is wear
}
head(data)
            timestamp  ac axis1 axis2 axis3 choi_wear
1 2012-06-27 10:54:00 404   207   218   270      TRUE
2 2012-06-27 10:55:00 409   169   257   270      TRUE
3 2012-06-27 10:56:00   0     0     0     0      TRUE
4 2012-06-27 10:57:00 341   157   174   248      TRUE
5 2012-06-27 10:58:00 281    23    23   279      TRUE
6 2012-06-27 10:59:00   0     0     0     0      TRUE
data %>% 
  count(choi_wear)
  choi_wear    n
1     FALSE  157
2      TRUE 1342

We can visualize the nonwear period detected by highlighting in yellow:

data %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = timestamp, y = ac)) + 
  geom_line() +
  geom_rect(data = choi_nonwear,
            aes(xmin = period_start,
                xmax = period_end,
                ymin = -Inf,
                ymax = Inf),
            alpha = 0.5,
           fill = "#F1C40FFF",
           inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "Activity Counts (AC)", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

The Choi algorithm is also implemented in the wearMarking function in the PhysicalActivity package. There are many other methods for nonwear detection, see Syed 2020 for a comparison of some methods.

Sleep

Like nonwear, there are many options for sleep detection. Here we will just show sleep detection using the Cole-Kripke algorithm, implemented in actigraph.sleepr::apply_cole_kripke.

data = ac60 %>%
  rename(timestamp = time) %>% 
  janitor::clean_names()
ck = actigraph.sleepr::apply_cole_kripke(data)
head(ck)
            timestamp  ac axis1 axis2 axis3 count sleep
1 2012-06-27 10:54:00 404   207   218   270  2.07     S
2 2012-06-27 10:55:00 409   169   257   270  1.69     S
3 2012-06-27 10:56:00   0     0     0     0  0.00     S
4 2012-06-27 10:57:00 341   157   174   248  1.57     S
5 2012-06-27 10:58:00 281    23    23   279  0.23     S
6 2012-06-27 10:59:00   0     0     0     0  0.00     S

We see there’s now a sleep column in the data that is either S (sleep) or W (wake).

ck %>% 
  count(sleep)
  sleep   n
1     S 939
2     W 560

We can plot the sleep/wake predictions. First we need to make a data frame with the sleep period start/ends.

sleep_periods = 
  ck %>% 
  mutate(sleep_period = data.table::rleid(sleep)) %>% 
  group_by(sleep_period) %>% 
  summarize(period_start = min(timestamp),
            period_end = max(timestamp),
            sleep = first(sleep),
            .groups = "drop")
  
data %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = timestamp, y = ac)) + 
  geom_line() +
  geom_rect(data = sleep_periods %>% filter(sleep == "S"),
            aes(xmin = period_start,
                xmax = period_end,
                ymin = -Inf,
                ymax = Inf),
            alpha = 0.5,
           fill = "#F39C12FF",
           inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "Activity Counts (AC)", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

We see that most of these highlighted areas are probably not sleep. We can use the Tudor-Locke algorithm on the output of the Cole-Kripke algorithm to detect bedtime and sleep time.

The object returned by actigraph.sleepr::apply_tudor_locke has columns about time of sleep start/end (in_bed_time, out_bed_time, onset, duration) and sleep summary metrics like movement_index and fragmentation_index; see the documentation for a full description of all columns. If the the input data are grouped, the output will have one row per group.

sleep_periods_tl = 
  actigraph.sleepr::apply_tudor_locke(ck)

sleep_periods_tl
# A tibble: 1 × 15
  in_bed_time         out_bed_time        onset               latency efficiency
  <dttm>              <dttm>              <dttm>                <int>      <dbl>
1 2012-06-28 00:02:00 2012-06-28 07:23:00 2012-06-28 00:02:00       0       99.8
# ℹ 10 more variables: duration <int>, activity_counts <int>,
#   nonzero_epochs <int>, total_sleep_time <int>, wake_after_onset <int>,
#   nb_awakenings <int>, ave_awakening <dbl>, movement_index <dbl>,
#   fragmentation_index <dbl>, sleep_fragmentation_index <dbl>

We can plot the sleep period:

data %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = timestamp, y = ac)) + 
  geom_line() +
  geom_rect(data = sleep_periods_tl,
            aes(xmin = onset,
                xmax = onset + as.period(duration, unit = "minutes"),
                ymin = -Inf,
                ymax = Inf),
            alpha = 0.5,
           fill = "#F39C12FF",
           inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "Activity Counts (AC)", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

Note that the nonwear period is scored as sleep by this algorithm, so in practice, we should remove nonwear periods first before applying the sleep detection algorithm.

```{r load packages} 
#| include: false 
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)
library(patchwork)
library(SummarizedActigraphy)
```

This tutorial will focus on generating minute-level Activity Counts^[[https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-16003-x](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-16003-x)] and steps from an ActiGraph GT3X file. While this pipeline is not comprehensive, it includes the basic steps that are necessary to process raw accelerometry data into minute-level summaries. 

::: {.callout-note}
The `.gt3x` [file format](https://github.com/actigraph/GT3X-File-Format) is used by ActiGraph accelerometers and contains raw accelerometer data along with metadata including timestamps and device information. Accelerometry data may be provided in other formats, such as `.csv`, but will typically include timestamps, values for acceleration in the X, Y, and Z dimensions, and metadata like participant ID. 
:::


First, we download a GT3X file from the [ActiGraph website](https://actigraphcorp.my.site.com/support/s/article/GT3X-ActiSleep-Sample-Data). The file contains approximately one day of data. 

## Download file 

```{r download data}
gt3x_file_raw = here::here("data", "accel_data_raw", "GT3X+ (01 day).gt3x")
gt3x_file = here::here("data", "accel_data_raw", "sample_data.gt3x")

if(!file.exists(gt3x_file)){
  url = "http://dl.theactigraph.com/demo/files/GT3XPlus-RawData(1-20).zip"

  out_file = here::here("data", "accel_data_raw.zip")
  if(!file.exists(out_file)){
    curl::curl_download(url, out_file, mode = "wb")
  }
  
  zip_file = here::here("data", "accel_data_raw.zip")
  out_dir  = here::here("data", "accel_data_raw")
  
  if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) {
    dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)
  }
  
  zip_list = unzip(zip_file, list = TRUE)
  
  unzip(zip_file, files = zip_list[1]$Name, exdir = out_dir)
  file.rename(gt3x_file_raw, gt3x_file)
}

```

## Read in the data 

We read in the data using the `read.gt3x` package. We read in as a dataframe instead of matrix (`asDataFrame = TRUE`) and impute any missing values with zeroes (`imputeZeroes = TRUE`).  The `read.gt3x::read.gt3x` function will read in the data and return a `data.frame` with columns for time, X, Y, Z, and other metadata.  The time column is in POSIXct format.



```{r read in gt3x}
#| cache: true
df = read.gt3x::read.gt3x(path = gt3x_file,
                          asDataFrame = TRUE,
                          imputeZeroes = TRUE)

```

## Get to know the data

The columns in the data are `time`, `X`, `Y`, and `Z`. Regardless of whether the data came from a GT3X file or other format, the next steps assume the data is in a `data.frame` format with columns for timestamp and the three acceleration axes. 

```{r}
head(df)
```

The data frame also has attributes that provide additional information about the data. The most important attributes are `sample_rate` and  `acceleration_min`/`acceleration_max`. Many functions for processing the raw data require the `sample_rate`; alternatively, the sample rate can be estimated from the timestamps if they are uniform. The `acceleration_min` and `acceleration_max` attributes provide the minimum and maximum acceleration values that the device can measure, which is important for calculating minute-level metrics like Activity Counts or Monitor Independent Movement Summary [(MIMS)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8301210/). 



```{r}
attributes(df) %>% names
attr(df, "sample_rate")
```


::: {.callout-tip}
When working with sub-second level data, make sure to set option `digits.secs = 3`. This allows us to make sure that milliseconds haven't been truncated. Truncation can occur during conversion from timestamp types or when writing and then reading from other data formats (e.g. CSV). Failure to account for milliseconds properly can cause problems when joining/merging based on timestamps.
:::


```{r}
options(digits.secs = 3)
head(df$time)
```


### A note on time zones 

When using the `read.gt3x` package, the time zone of the output data is always `GMT`. Which time zone the data were collected may be contained in the header; in this case however, it is not. 

```{r}
attr_list = attributes(df)
attr_list$header$TimeZone
```

::: {.callout-important}
All timestamps are in local time (of the device) even though they are represented as `POSIXct` with `GMT` timezone [in the data]; see documentation [here](https://github.com/THLfi/read.gt3x/blob/a41037a5ab1390b5393ee09efacac08a44432a77/R/readGT3X.R#L9). Let's go through an explicit example. 

+ A user starts recording data with a GT3X device at 8AM in New York City in June (Eastern Daylight Time Zone, UTC-6). 
+ In the data, the timestamp will be recorded as `08:00 GMT`
:::


You can set the data to the correct timezone with `lubridate::tz`. The `with_tz` and `force_tz` functions can change the timestamp the data in different ways (changing attribute vs. changing data).  

Here we illustrate the difference between changing the attribute and changing the data. Let's take a subset of the times and show the time zone (GMT). 

```{r}
times = head(df$time)
times
tz(times)
```

The `force_tz`, and  `tz(x) <-` functions assign a specified timezone to the object.


```{r}
times_edt = times # make a copy of the times 
tz(times_edt) <- "America/New_York"; times_edt
force_tz(times, "America/New_York")
```

We see that the result is the time itself hasn't changed but the time zone attachd is `EDT` instead of `GMT`. Tge data still indicates hour minute `10:54`, but in a different timezone.

The `with_tz` function projects the data into a timezone, but the actual moment of time does not change:

```{r}
with_tz(times, "America/New_York")
```

Now the data displays hour `06:54` as this shifts the data from GMT.  We can see that `force_tz` doesn't change the way the data is stored, just the way it is displayed, but `with_tz` changes the way the data is both stored and displayed.

```{r}
as.numeric(times_edt)
as.numeric(force_tz(times, "America/New_York"))
as.numeric(with_tz(times, "America/New_York"))
```

:::{.callout-warning}
Takehome message: Use caution with time zones, especially in the presence of data from different devices and when merging data with timestamps, such as merging with GPS or heart rate data. Shifting time may project some data into a different day/date, which is highly relevant since many summary measures are done at a day/date level. Non-GT3X files and packages other than `read.gt3x` may handle time zones differently, so be sure to check the documentation.
:::

### Plotting the data 

Before we do anything else, let's plot the data. We have `r nrow(df)` observations, so we'll want to start with plotting a subset only. We pivot the data longer for easier plotting and plot the first five minutes of observations. 

```{r}
#| cache: true 
long = df %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = X:Z, names_to = "axis", values_to = "accel")

long %>% 
  filter(between(time, floor_date(time[1]), #keep only first 5 minutes
                   floor_date(time[1]) + as.period(5, "minutes"))) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = accel, colour = axis)) + 
    geom_line() + # add acceleration, can also do `geom_step`
    theme(legend.position = "inside", 
          legend.position.inside = c(0.6, 0.78),
          panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  paletteer::scale_color_paletteer_d("ggthemr::flat", name = "Axis") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "1 min")+
  labs(y = "Acceleration (g)", x = "Time") 
  

```

We see that at the beginning of the data, all acceleration values are zero. We'll discuss this in the context of idle sleep mode. 


## Handling idle sleep mode 

Idle sleep mode is an option for ActiGraph devices set when recording. When a device hasn't moved for a period of time, it does not record any measurements until the device moves again. This is done to preserve battery life. 

[ActiGraph documentation](https://actigraphcorp.my.site.com/support/s/article/Idle-Sleep-Mode-Explained) explains idle sleep mode as follows: 

> For example, a device set to sample at 30Hz would store the last known accelerometer reading 30 times every second; the device would then wake up and check for movement.  If no movement were detected, this pattern would continue.  Otherwise the unit would exit sleep mode (i.e., "wake up") and continue sampling in normal fashion.

Thus, if idle sleep mode activates on a device, there will be a gap in time in the measurements. While this is an accurate representation of the data, it causes issues for methods that rely on continuous measurements. The `imputeZeroes` argument in `read.gt3x` fills in missing measurements with `0` for all axes. This zeroes are not always from idle sleep mode: for example, they could also be from charging events. The `flag_idle_sleep` (default `FALSE`) argument in `read.gt3x` outputs an indicator column of `idle` or not and is useful for identifying segments of data that are in idle sleep mode. We see that the first few seconds of our data are in idle sleep mode: 

```{r read_flagged_data}
df_flagged = read.gt3x::read.gt3x(path = gt3x_file, 
                                  asDataFrame = TRUE, 
                                  imputeZeroes = TRUE,
                                  flag_idle_sleep = TRUE)
head(df_flagged)
```


```{r}
long_flag = df_flagged %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = X:Z, names_to = "axis", values_to = "accel")

idle_df = df_flagged %>% 
  filter(between(time, floor_date(time[1]), #keep only first 5 minutes
                   floor_date(time[1]) + as.period(5, "minutes"))) %>% 
  filter(idle == TRUE) 

long_flag %>% 
  filter(between(time, floor_date(time[1]), #keep only first 5 minutes
                   floor_date(time[1]) + as.period(5, "minutes"))) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = accel, colour = axis)) + 
    geom_line() + # add acceleration, can also do `geom_step`
    annotate(geom = "rect",
             xmin = min(idle_df$time),
             xmax = max(idle_df$time),
             ymin = -3,
             ymax = 3,
             fill = "pink", 
             alpha = .8) +
    theme(legend.position = "inside", 
          legend.position.inside = c(0.6, 0.78),
          panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  paletteer::scale_color_paletteer_d("ggthemr::flat", name = "Axis") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "1 min")+
  labs(y = "Acceleration (g)", x = "Time") 
```

There's also at least one more instance of idle sleep mode: 

```{r}
idle_df_notstart = df_flagged %>% 
  filter(!between(time, floor_date(time[1]), #keep only first 5 minutes
                   floor_date(time[1]) + as.period(5, "minutes"))) %>% 
  filter(idle == TRUE) 

segments_idle = 
  idle_df_notstart %>% 
  mutate(lag = as.numeric(difftime(time, lag(time), units = "secs")),
         lag = lag < .05,
         group = data.table::rleid(lag))


##11:20 to 11:50
long %>% 
  filter(between(time, as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 11:20:00", tz = "GMT"),
                 as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 11:50:00", tz = "GMT"))) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = accel, colour = axis)) + 
    geom_line() + # add acceleration, can also do `geom_step`
    annotate(geom = "rect",
             xmin = min(segments_idle$time[segments_idle$group == 2]),
             xmax = max(segments_idle$time[segments_idle$group == 2]),
             ymin = -3,
             ymax = 3,
             fill = "pink", 
             alpha = .7) +
    theme(legend.position = "inside", 
          legend.position.inside = c(0.6, 0.9),
          panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  paletteer::scale_color_paletteer_d("ggthemr::flat", name = "Axis") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "5 min")+
  labs(y = "Acceleration (g)", x = "Time") 
```

There are a few options for handling data in idle sleep mode:

+ Leave gaps in the data 
+ Fill in `NA` values for these segments
+ Fill in `0` values for these segments,
+ Last observation carried forward (LOCF)

::: {.table}
| Method   | Issues |
|---------|---------|
| Leave gaps in data  | Most software assumes continuous time, missing time may cause errors 
| Fill in `NA` values  | Some software assumes no missing data  |
| Fill in `0` values   | Not accurate because gravity is being exerted on the device, can cause sharp changes in the signal which can induce higher variance than is correct (going from value to `0`) |
| Last observation carried forward (LOCF)   | Not "real" values, harder to identify non-wear after the fact if not flagged appropriately |
:::

:::{.callout-note}
The LOCF approach is such that if the last measurement before non-measurement on an axis was `0.952` for example, the value of `0.952` will be repeated for each sample until the device moves. Each axis is handled separately (no information for X is used for Y). This procedure is done for all axes.  
:::


Our recommendation is to use the LOCF approach. It is consistent with the ActiGraph documentation, induces a variance of 0 during the idle sleep interval, has no jump discontinuity from previous measurements, provides continuous signal, and can be flagged.  Summary measures of activity (e.g. Activity Counts, Activity Index) should provide an appropriate summary value of $0$ to this zero variance data.

There are packages that implement LOCF on this type of data, but we can also do it using some straightforward `tidyverse` functions.  We find records where all axes have an acceleration of $0$, replace those acceleration values for those records with `NA` and fill in the data (using LOCF) using `tidyr::fill`.

```{r save_xdf}
#| echo: false
xdf = df
```

```{r fill_data}
sample_rate = attr(df, "sample_rate")
acceleration_max = as.numeric(attr(df, "acceleration_max"))
df = dplyr::as_tibble(df)
df = df %>% 
  mutate(all_zero = X == 0 & Y == 0 & Z == 0) %>%  # flag where all zeroes
  mutate( # replace all 0 with NA so it can be filled  
    X = ifelse(all_zero, NA_real_, X),
    Y = ifelse(all_zero, NA_real_, Y),
    Z = ifelse(all_zero, NA_real_, Z)
  )
any(df$all_zero)
df = df %>% 
  select(-all_zero) %>% # remove this column
  tidyr::fill(X, Y, Z, .direction = "down") # fill down using LOCF (time sorted)
head(df)
```

If the first records are in idle sleep mode, they will have no "before value" to fill in and will continue to be `NA` given this code.  To handle this last case we can replace these values using `tidyr::fill` with the direction of "up" to make a flat starting signal or with $0$ for simplicity (done here):

```{r na_replace}
df = df %>% tidyr::replace_na(list(X = 0, Y = 0, Z = 0))
```

This ensures that every record has a numeric value.  Users can also drop those first records.

Now we can see that the signal has been filled in for those segments that were previously all $0$.


```{r}
long = df %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = X:Z, names_to = "axis", values_to = "accel")

long %>% 
  filter(between(time, as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 11:20:00", tz = "GMT"),
                 as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 11:50:00", tz = "GMT"))) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = accel, colour = axis)) + 
    geom_line() + # add acceleration, can also do `geom_step`
    annotate(geom = "rect",
             xmin = min(segments_idle$time[segments_idle$group == 2]),
             xmax = max(segments_idle$time[segments_idle$group == 2]),
             ymin = -3,
             ymax = 3,
             fill = "pink", 
             alpha = .7) +
    theme(legend.position = "inside", 
          legend.position.inside = c(0.6, 0.9),
          panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  paletteer::scale_color_paletteer_d("ggthemr::flat", name = "Axis") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "5 min")+
  labs(y = "Acceleration (g)", x = "Time") 
```

## Gravity Calibration

Gravity correction/calibration corrects issues in the data that may arise from miscalibration of a device. Accelerometry is measured in $g$, and we assume that gravity values for each person are the same if another device was used or the same device was used at a different location. Thus gravity correction can help harmonize data that is different due to non-biological or systemic effects.

The most common gravity correction method estimates shift and scale parameters to transform the data and will therefore only affect downstream metrics that are not invariant to scaling and shifting. The correction should be small compared to the magnitude of the signal. 

:::{.callout-note}
Not all pipelines employ gravity correction, including many pipelines for ActiGraph data.
:::

We will use the method employed in GGIR^[[https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/japplphysiol.00421.2014](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/japplphysiol.00421.2014)]. 


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### More about gravity calibration
The calibration is done by estimating how much of the data is projected onto the unit sphere (radius of length 1 for all 3 axes).

The procedure below looks for when the standard deviation of the signal was <13 m$g$ (milli-$g$) in all three axes within a time window.  The 13 m$g$ cutoff was selected to be just above the empirically derived baseline (noise) standard deviation of 10 m$g$ to retain only non-movement periods. A window of length 10 seconds is used.
:::


The `GGIR::g.calibrate` function takes in a data filename and calculates the calibration parameters.  We recommend to input the output of `g.inspectfile` that provides metadata and a specification of the file being calibrated.  Since we have an older GT3X file that can't be directly read in by GGIR, we first use the `SummarizedActigraphy` package to write to csv, then use GGIR for calibration. We use `imputeZeroes=FALSE` because we don't want the calibration to use any data from idle sleep mode. 

We can download the `SummarizedActigraphy` package from [Github](https://github.com/muschellij2/SummarizedActigraphy) first: 

```{r}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("muschellij2/SummarizedActigraphy")
```

Then apply calibration: 

```{r calibrate}
#| cache: true
library(GGIR)
df_nozero = read.gt3x::read.gt3x(path = gt3x_file, 
                      asDataFrame = TRUE,
                      imputeZeroes = FALSE)

outfile = SummarizedActigraphy::write_acc_csv(df_nozero, 
                                              tempfile(fileext = ".csv"))
info = GGIR::g.inspectfile(outfile)
csv_calibration_params = GGIR::g.calibrate(
  datafile = outfile,
  inspectfileobject = info)
```


The parameters denotes how many hours of data was used:

```{r calibrate_n_hours}
csv_calibration_params$nhoursused
```

What the estimated calibration error was for all non-movement windows before and after calibration to the unit sphere:

```{r calibrate_cal_error}
csv_calibration_params$cal.error.start
csv_calibration_params$cal.error.end
```

In this case, we see that: 

```{r}
csv_calibration_params$QCmessage
```

Therefore the scale and shift parameters are $1$ and $0$ in all three dimensions: 

```{r calibrate_cal_estimates}
csv_calibration_params[c("scale", "offset")]
```

We'll still illustrate how to calibrate the data by using the  `scale` function and  performing the subtraction/division:

```{r df_calibrated}
df_calibrated = df
df_calibrated[, c("X", "Y", "Z")] = scale(
  df[, c("X", "Y", "Z")], 
  center = -csv_calibration_params$offset, 
  scale = 1/csv_calibration_params$scale)
```

## Calculating Activity Counts 


Activity Counts (AC) are a measure of physical activity. Previously they were a proprietary output of the ActiLife software, but the ActiGraph team published a [paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-16003-x]) in 2022 that describes how they are calculated and released the `agcounts` Python module to calculate them^[[https://github.com/actigraph/agcounts](https://github.com/actigraph/agcounts)].  The `agcounts`, `actilifecounts`, and [`agcounter`](https://github.com/muschellij2/agcounter) packages have functions that can convert the raw data into minute-level counts. The `actilifecounts` implements the method in native R code, `agcounts`/`agcounter` wraps the Python code into an R interface.

Calculating AC from these packages gives a per-axis AC measure.  Axis-level AC can be aggregated from higher resolutions to lower: if you calculate AC at 15 second intervals, then the 60 second/minute level AC is the sum of the 4 values measured at 15 seconds.  Once AC is aggregated at the desired epoch, the AC units from the axes are combined into a vector magnitude for a single summary:

$$
AC = \sqrt{(AC_{x}^2 + AC_{y}^2 + AC_{z}^2)}
$$

Typically, we calculate counts for 60-second (1 minute) epochs. We can pass in the timezone of the data to ensure the desired time stamps. We use the calibrated data and have to first convert to data frame, then rename columns for consistency. 

```{r run_ac60}
#| cache: true

df_calibrated = df_calibrated %>% 
  as.data.frame()
ac60 = df_calibrated %>% 
  agcounts::calculate_counts(epoch = 60L, tz = lubridate::tz(df_calibrated$time))
head(ac60)

ac60 = 
  ac60 %>% 
  select(time, AC = Vector.Magnitude, everything())

# save for later analysis 
out_dir = here::here("data", "accel_outputs")
if(!dir.exists(out_dir)) dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)

out_file = here::here(out_dir, "minute_level_ac.rds")
if(!file.exists(out_file)) {
  readr::write_rds(ac60,
                   out_file,
                   compress = "xz")
}
```

:::{.callout-note}
The AC algorithm resamples the data to 30Hz. The original algorithm provided in the `agcounts` Python module only correctly handled sample rates that were measured at round intervals (e.g. 30, 40, ..., 90, 100).
:::

Let's plot the AC with some thresholds for physical activity levels. While many different thresholds can be used, the Montoye^[ [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32677510/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32677510/)] thresholds are a common choice.

:::{.callout-note}
### More about thresholds 
The Montoye thresholds were developed by observing $n=47$ participants in both laboratory and free-living settings. Activity intensity was determined through direct observation and then mapped to the AC measured by wrist-worn accelerometers to develop cut points for each activity intensity. The cut points had an accuracy of $70$\% in free-living. The Montoye thresholds are specific to Activity Counts, but [another paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9356340/) has mapped the AC thresholds to other activity summaries, including Monitor Independent Movement Summaries (MIMS; see below) and Euclidian Norm Minus One (ENMO)^[[https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0164045](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0164045)]. 
:::


```{r}
ac60 %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = AC)) + 
  geom_line() +
  annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 0,
           ymax = 2860,
           fill = "#3498DBFF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
  annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 2861,
           ymax = 3940,
           fill = "#F39C12FF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
   annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 3941,
           ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#E74C3CFF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "Activity Counts (AC)", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 1430,
           label = "Sedentary") + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 3300,
           label = "Light") + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 7000,
           label = "Moderate-vigorous")


  
```

## Calculating other outputs 

### MIMS 

Monitor Independent Movement Summary (MIMS)^[[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34308270/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34308270/)] are an open-source summary of physical activity. They were used in the NHANES accelerometry study from 2011-2014^[[https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2011/DataFiles/PAXMIN_G.htm](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2011/DataFiles/PAXMIN_G.htm)]. We can calculate MIMS using the `MIMSunit` package; this requires `acceleration_max` variables from the header. 


```{r calculate_mims}
#| cache: true
dynamic_range = c(-acceleration_max, acceleration_max)
df_mims = df_calibrated %>% 
  rename(HEADER_TIME_STAMP = time) %>% 
  MIMSunit::mims_unit(dynamic_range = dynamic_range, epoch = "1 min")

## save for later analysis 
out_file = here::here(out_dir, "minute_level_mims.rds")
if(!file.exists(out_file)) {
  readr::write_rds(df_mims %>% rename(time = HEADER_TIME_STAMP, mims = MIMS_UNIT),
                   out_file,
                   compress = "xz")
}
```

Note, as this resamples data to 100Hz, this may have a significantly larger memory footprint for processing than the raw data.  We can see the output from the MIMS processing:

```{r mims_show}
head(df_mims)
```

We can plot the MIMS, using thresholds mapped from the AC thresholds^[[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9356340/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9356340/)]. 

```{r}
df_mims %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = HEADER_TIME_STAMP, y = MIMS_UNIT)) + 
  geom_line() +
  annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 0,
           ymax = 15.047,
           fill = "#3498DBFF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
  annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 15.048,
           ymax = 19.614,
           fill = "#F39C12FF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
   annotate(geom = "rect",
           xmin = min(df$time),
           xmax = max(df$time),
           ymin = 19.615,
           ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#E74C3CFF",
           alpha = 0.5) + 
  labs(y = "MIMS", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 8,
           label = "Sedentary") + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 17,
           label = "Light") + 
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = min(df$time) + lubridate::hours(16),
           y = 23,
           label = "Moderate-vigorous") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "MIMS", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) 

```


### Steps 

Steps can be estimated from raw accelerometry data using several different open source algorithms. Here we'll focus on two algorithms: the machine learning based [`stepcount` algorithm](https://github.com/OxWearables/stepcount), which is implemented in Python. The Python module provides two machine learning algorithms (self-supervised learner [SSL] and random forest [RF]) that estimate steps from raw accelerometry. 

The [`stepcount`](https://github.com/jhuwit/stepcount) R package wraps this Python code. The package also has functions for creating a Conda environment for these functions, as many different Python modules have different requirements - the `walking` package has similar functionality.

You need to first create the conda environment: 

```{r}
#| eval: false

library(stepcount)
envname = "stepcount"
reticulate::conda_create(envname = envname, packages = c("python=3.9", "openjdk", "pip"))
Sys.unsetenv("RETICULATE_PYTHON")
reticulate::use_condaenv(envname)
reticulate::py_install("stepcount", envname = envname, method = "conda", pip = TRUE)
```

Then we can check we have everything in order: 

```{r}
stepcount::unset_reticulate_python()
stepcount::use_stepcount_condaenv()
library(reticulate)
stepcount::stepcount_check() 
```


Then we can run the model, using the SSL model type. We have to include the sample rate as well. Since the method does it's own gravity calibration, we use the uncalibrated dataset. To make knitting faster, we save the output. 

```{r run_stepcount_ex}
out = here::here("tutorials", "data", "sc_out.rds")
if(!dir.exists(dirname(out))) dir.create(dirname(out))

if(!file.exists(out)){
  ssl = stepcount::stepcount(df, sample_rate = sample_rate, model_type = "ssl")
  readr::write_rds(ssl, out)
}
ssl = readr::read_rds(out)
```


The output of `stepcount` is a list of different pieces of information, including information about the device:

```{r stepcount_output}
names(ssl)
```

We are most interested in the `data.frame` of estimated steps with associated timestamps:

```{r stepcount_steps}
head(ssl$steps)
```

and similarly a `data.frame` of flagged time for walking:

```{r stepcount_walking}
head(ssl$walking)
```

The `stepcount` method estimates steps in 10-second windows, which we can aggregate into minutes:


```{r sc_steps_minute}
ssl_60 = ssl$steps %>% 
  mutate(time = floor_date(time, "1 minute")) %>% 
  group_by(time) %>% 
  summarise(ssl_steps = sum(steps), .groups = "drop")
head(ssl_60)
```

We can fit the random forest too: 


```{r rf_steps}
out = here::here("tutorials", "data", "rf_out.rds")

if(!file.exists(out)){
  rf = stepcount::stepcount(df, sample_rate = sample_rate, model_type = "rf")
  readr::write_rds(rf, out)
}
rf = readr::read_rds(out)

rf_60 = 
  rf$steps %>% 
  mutate(time = floor_date(time, "1 minute")) %>% 
  group_by(time) %>% 
  summarise(rf_steps = sum(steps), .groups = "drop")
```


We can plot the results; we see a large difference between number steps identified by each method! 

```{r plot_steps}
steps_joined = 
  rf_60 %>% 
  full_join(ssl_60, by = "time")

steps_joined %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = contains("steps"),
               names_to = "method", 
               values_to = "steps") %>% 
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = c("ssl_steps", "rf_steps"), labels = c("SSL", "RF"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = steps, color = method)) + 
  geom_step() +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "Steps per Minute", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#9B59B6FF", "#D35400FF"),
                     labels = c("SSL", "RF"),
                     name = "Method") + 
  facet_grid(method~.)
```

Finally, we can zoom in on a walking period: 

```{r walking_period}
joined_seconds =
  ssl$steps %>% rename(ssl_steps = steps) %>% 
  full_join(rf$steps %>% rename(rf_steps = steps), by = "time") %>% 
  filter(rf_steps > 0 & ssl_steps > 0)


xdf = 
  joined_seconds %>% 
  mutate(end = time + as.period(10, "seconds")) %>% 
  filter(time >= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:53:40", tz = "GMT") & 
         end <= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:54:40", tz = "GMT"))

p1 = df %>% 
  mutate(vm = sqrt(X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2)) %>% 
  filter(time >= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:53:50", tz = "GMT") & 
         time <= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:54:40", tz = "GMT")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = vm)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "5 secs", date_labels = "%H:%M:%S") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Time of day", y = "Acceleration (g)", title = "RF Steps") +
  geom_rect(data = xdf, 
            aes(xmin = time, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = rf_steps), 
             alpha = 0.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis(limits = c(9, 20), name = "Steps per 10 second window",
                              breaks = seq(10, 20, 2))

p2 = df %>% 
  mutate(vm = sqrt(X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2)) %>% 
  filter(time >= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:53:50", tz = "GMT") & 
         time <= as.POSIXct("2012-06-27 16:54:40", tz = "GMT")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = vm)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "5 secs", date_labels = "%H:%M:%S") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Time of day", y = "Acceleration (g)", title = "SSL Steps") +
  geom_rect(data = xdf, 
            aes(xmin = time, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = ssl_steps), 
             alpha = 0.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis(limits = c(9, 20), name = "Steps per 10 second window",
                              breaks = seq(10, 20, 2))


p1 / p2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect", axes = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r save_walking}
## save results for downstream analysis
out_file = here::here(out_dir, "minute_level_steps.rds")
if(!file.exists(out_file)) {
  readr::write_rds(steps_joined,
                   out_file,
                   compress = "xz")
}

```


### Nonwear and Sleep

The `actigraph.sleepr` package implements three sleep scoring/detection algorithms: Sadeh^[[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7939118/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7939118/)], Cole-Kripke^[[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1455130/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1455130/)] and Tudor-Locke^[[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24383507/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24383507/)] as well as two non-wear detection algorithms: Troiano^[[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18091006/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18091006/)] and Choi^[[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20581716/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20581716/)].

We can download the package from Github: 

```{r}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("dipetkov/actigraph.sleepr")
```

#### Nonwear 

We will demonstrate using the Choi algorithm to find nonwear. We will run this on the minute-level AC data, *not* the raw accelerometry data. 

We need to rename the `time` column to `timestamp` and make all column names lowercase. 


```{r choi_data}
data = ac60 %>%
  rename(timestamp = time) %>% 
  janitor::clean_names()
```


```{r choi}
choi_nonwear = actigraph.sleepr::apply_choi(data, use_magnitude = TRUE)
head(choi_nonwear)
```
The default for `use_magnitude` is `FALSE`, which means that only the `axis1` is used to measure activity. We set `use_magnitude = TRUE` so that the magnitude of the vector (axis1, axis2, axis3) is used instead. 

The output is a `data.frame` with the start and stop times of non-wear, along with the length of the nonwear interval. 

We see that the output is a `data.frame` of start and stop times of non-wear.  We can expand this to a sequence of times and merge with the minute level counts, creating a column with an indicator for wear. 

```{r}
if (nrow(choi_nonwear) == 0) {
  data$choi_wear = TRUE
} else {
  choi_df = purrr::map2_df(
    choi_nonwear$period_start, choi_nonwear$period_end,
    function(from, to) {
      data.frame(timestamp = seq(from, to, by = 60L), # need this name to align
                 choi_wear = FALSE)
    })
  data = left_join(data, choi_df) %>%
    tidyr::replace_na(list(choi_wear = TRUE)) # default is wear
}
head(data)
data %>% 
  count(choi_wear)
```
We can visualize the nonwear period detected by highlighting in yellow: 

```{r}
data %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = timestamp, y = ac)) + 
  geom_line() +
  geom_rect(data = choi_nonwear,
            aes(xmin = period_start,
                xmax = period_end,
                ymin = -Inf,
                ymax = Inf),
            alpha = 0.5,
           fill = "#F1C40FFF",
           inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "Activity Counts (AC)", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```
The Choi algorithm is also implemented in the `wearMarking` function in the [`PhysicalActivity`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/PhysicalActivity/index.html) package. There are many other methods for nonwear detection, see [Syed 2020](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-62821-2) for a comparison of some methods. 


#### Sleep 

Like nonwear, there are many options for sleep detection. Here we will just show sleep detection using the Cole-Kripke algorithm, implemented in `actigraph.sleepr::apply_cole_kripke`.


```{r redata_ac60}
data = ac60 %>%
  rename(timestamp = time) %>% 
  janitor::clean_names()
```

```{r sleep_ck}
ck = actigraph.sleepr::apply_cole_kripke(data)
head(ck)
```

We see there's now a `sleep` column in the data that is either `S` (sleep) or `W` (wake). 

```{r}
ck %>% 
  count(sleep)
```


We can plot the sleep/wake predictions. First we need to make a data frame with the sleep period start/ends. 

```{r ck_plot}
sleep_periods = 
  ck %>% 
  mutate(sleep_period = data.table::rleid(sleep)) %>% 
  group_by(sleep_period) %>% 
  summarize(period_start = min(timestamp),
            period_end = max(timestamp),
            sleep = first(sleep),
            .groups = "drop")
  
data %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = timestamp, y = ac)) + 
  geom_line() +
  geom_rect(data = sleep_periods %>% filter(sleep == "S"),
            aes(xmin = period_start,
                xmax = period_end,
                ymin = -Inf,
                ymax = Inf),
            alpha = 0.5,
           fill = "#F39C12FF",
           inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "Activity Counts (AC)", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
 
```


We see that most of these highlighted areas are probably *not* sleep. We can use the Tudor-Locke algorithm on the output of the Cole-Kripke algorithm to detect bedtime and sleep time. 

The object returned by `actigraph.sleepr::apply_tudor_locke` has columns about time of sleep start/end (`in_bed_time`, `out_bed_time`, `onset`, `duration`) and sleep summary metrics like `movement_index` and `fragmentation_index`; see the documentation for a full description of all columns. If the the input data are grouped, the output will have one row per group.

```{r}
sleep_periods_tl = 
  actigraph.sleepr::apply_tudor_locke(ck)

sleep_periods_tl
```
We can plot the sleep period: 

```{r}
data %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = timestamp, y = ac)) + 
  geom_line() +
  geom_rect(data = sleep_periods_tl,
            aes(xmin = onset,
                xmax = onset + as.period(duration, unit = "minutes"),
                ymin = -Inf,
                ymax = Inf),
            alpha = 0.5,
           fill = "#F39C12FF",
           inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "2 hours") +
  labs(y = "Activity Counts (AC)", x = "Time") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())


```

Note that the nonwear period is scored as sleep by this algorithm, so in practice, we should remove nonwear periods first before applying the sleep detection algorithm.
